children: US soybean futures fell for a fourth straight day on Thursday and touched a seven-week low as active harvesting of what is forecast to be a record
crop offset support from renewed Chinese demand, analysts said.

Corn futures were mixed after hitting a two-month low last week as traders assessed harvest progress, while wheat advanced as the latest attacks on Black Sea shipping reinforced concerns about global supplies.

A recent stretch of dry weather around the US Midwest has allowed farmers to accelerate harvesting of summer crops, and many growers were gathering soybeans before corn. Rains slowed the pace of field work in the western Midwest on Thursday, but a drier pattern was expected in the upcoming week, forecasters said.

Chicago Board of Trade November soybeans (SX26) were down 8 cents at $12.69-1/4 a bushel by 11:30 a.m. CDT (1630 GMT). December corn (CZ26) was down 3/4 cent at $4.80 a bushel, holding within a recent tight trading range after plunging last week following an unexpectedly large harvest outlook from the US Department of Agriculture.
Soybeans shrugged off news of more US purchases by

as the pace of buying by the world's top importer has not been as strong as some traders anticipated. China agreed to buy 25 million metric tons annually during recent trade talks, according to the White House, and government data showed that the country has fulfilled about half of the commitment to date.
"It's good to see them buying, but it's not where we need to be," said Brodrick Schmidt, analyst with US Commodities.

The US domestic soybean crush last month also fell short of expectations, according to a monthly National Oilseed Processors Association report released on Thursday, which showed the September crush at a 13-month low of 196.3 million bushels.
CBOT December wheat futures (WZ26) were up 3 cents at $6.76-1/4 a bushel, supported by further attacks on cargo ships in the western Black Sea.
